title: Classical and Quantum PM2.5 Predictive Models
text:
🧠 Overview
This repository contains the reproducible and recovered computational materials associated with the article “Mathematical Evaluation of Classical and Quantum Predictive Models Applied to PM2.5 Forecasting in Urban Environments.”
The study compares two different predictive paradigms applied to real PM2.5 observations from the Plaza Castilla monitoring station in Madrid:

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) for continuous time-series prediction;
Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) for binary classification using quantum kernels.

The broader objective is not to treat both models as functionally equivalent, but to examine how classical and quantum approaches behave under the same environmental-data context in terms of predictive capability, classification performance and computational efficiency.

title: Analysis and Prediction of PM2.5 Pollution in Madrid
text:
🎯 Research motivation
Urban PM2.5 pollution remains an important environmental and public-health concern.
The project addresses three complementary questions:

How have PM2.5 concentrations evolved in Madrid over time?
How do pollution patterns differ across districts?
Can a hybrid Prophet-LSTM model provide useful forecasts for future PM2.5 levels?

The methodological emphasis is not limited to prediction. The analysis integrates data understanding, preprocessing, descriptive analysis, spatial interpretation and forecasting within a reproducible workflow.

title: Analysis and Prediction of PM2.5 Pollution in Madrid
text:
📌 Main findings

PM2.5 concentrations show a general downward trend from 2019 to mid-2024.
Important interannual fluctuations and pollution peaks remain.
PM2.5 behaviour differs across districts, supporting localised analysis.
Prophet-LSTM integrates explicit seasonal structure with nonlinear temporal dependencies.
Forecasts can support planning and environmental decision-making when interpreted together with uncertainty and local monitoring conditions.

text:
⚠️ Reproducibility notes
Two discrepancies in the published article are relevant when reconstructing the experiments:

Data splitting
The general methodology section describes an 80/20 split based on 330 observations.
The dedicated LSTM section instead describes 2017–2023 for training and 2024 for external testing.
The reconstructed LSTM script follows the dedicated LSTM section.


LSTM R²
The dedicated LSTM results table reports:
R² = 0.05
A later comparative table reports a different LSTM R² value.
The repository therefore uses the metric reported in the dedicated LSTM results section and flags the later discrepancy rather than attempting to resolve it retrospectively.

title: Classical and Quantum PM2.5 Predictive Models
text:
📈 Classical model: LSTM
The LSTM experiment uses the Plaza Castilla PM2.5 series to forecast continuous concentration values.
The published implementation describes a single LSTM layer with 64 units, followed by a dense output layer, trained for 50 epochs with the Adam optimizer and MSE loss after MinMax normalization.





Fig. 2. Observed and predicted PM2.5 values for the 2024 LSTM evaluation.
The article reports:

RMSE: 15.98 µg/m³
MAE: 4.42 µg/m³
R²: 0.05
Training time: 29.68 s
Peak memory: 53.22 MB

The main limitation is the underestimation of extreme pollution peaks.

title: Classical and Quantum PM2.5 Predictive Models
Classical and Quantum PM2.5 Predictive Models
text:
📌 Main interpretation
The two approaches solve different but complementary tasks.

LSTM preserves temporal continuity and provides continuous forecasts.
QSVM provides a threshold-based decision mechanism with strong class separation in the reported experiment.
LSTM is more informative for concentration trajectories, but struggles with extreme events.
QSVM is more limited in output type, but offers a compact decision boundary for threshold classification.
The study frames both paradigms as potentially complementary components of future hybrid environmental-intelligence systems.

🔬 Reproducibility status
The complete original computational environment was not preserved.
This repository therefore distinguishes between:

recovered code from the original Google Colab notebook;
reconstructed code based on the methodological details reported in the article;
and published results transcribed directly from the paper.

The Scripts and code provenance page documents this distinction explicitly.

title: Classical and Quantum PM2.5 Predictive Models
text:
⚠️ Published-method notes
The article contains two internal inconsistencies that are preserved transparently rather than silently reconciled:

the methodology section describes an 80/20 split of 330 daily observations, while the dedicated LSTM section describes 2017–2023 as training data and 2024 as an external test set;
the dedicated LSTM results table reports R² = 0.05, whereas the later comparative table contains a different value for the LSTM R² score.

For reproducibility purposes, this repository treats the model-specific LSTM section and its dedicated metrics table as the primary source for the reconstructed LSTM experiment.

⚛️ Quantum-kernel logic
The QSVM approach maps classical feature vectors into a quantum feature space and evaluates similarity through a quantum kernel.





Fig. 6. Pseudocode for estimating the quantum kernel from the fidelity between parameterised quantum states.
The article describes a Qiskit implementation using a ZFeatureMap, angle encoding and a statevector simulator.
The target variable is binarised using 25 µg/m³:

Class 0: PM2.5 ≤ 25 µg/m³
Class 1: PM2.5 > 25 µg/m³

title: Analytical Notebook
text:
🧭 Cross-paradigm interpretation
The comparison must be interpreted carefully because the models do not solve the same prediction task:

LSTM performs continuous regression over a temporal sequence;
QSVM performs binary classification relative to a pollution threshold.

The study therefore frames the comparison as cross-paradigm rather than as a strict like-for-like benchmark.
The main methodological value lies in showing how both approaches respond to the same environmental context under different operational objectives.
